# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...
2. Protect the states' right to act. ...
3. Whistleblower protections. ...

Respectfully, Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here . 
 You can read Congressman Obernolte’s and Congresswoman Trahan’s op-ed here .

 Frontier Developers 
 Entities that have trained a frontier model (a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ computing operations) AND had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior year (Sec. 101)
 A subset called "large frontier developers" must have had more than $500 million in gross revenue (Sec. 101)
 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms

 Federal Agencies

 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)

 House GAAIA Discussion Draft Proposes Federal AI Governance Framework

 June 16, 2026 

 Matthew Berlin 
 , 
 Danielle W. Bulger 
 , 
 Cissy Jackson 
 , 
 Emily B. Lewis 
 , 
 Natasha Weis 
 , 
 Nardeen Billan 
 , 
 Perry A. Jackson 

 Share This Page 

 Email 

 LinkedIn X Facebook 

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 If passed, GAAIA would authorize $100 million annually for CAISI for fisc

{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "<!-- DRAFT v1 — FRC policy team, for Executive Director sign-off Fri 23 Oct 2026. Not sent. -->
<!-- Note for ED: dateline set for Monday 26 Oct (transmittal week); adjust if sending on a different day. -->

**FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION**
[address line — office to insert]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comment of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking public comment before introduction. For a bill of this weight, that is the right way to work, and we take the invitation seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are Republicans, Democrats and independents. They are united by one belief: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory. We say that plainly because it is the fact Congress most needs to hear, and because the draft, read carefully, already agrees with us.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer provisions with a moratorium: an immediate pause on training the most powerful models until Congress certifies that systems of that class can be reliably controlled; a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be certified; and criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate the law. We explain our position section by section below, and we offer drafting language and staff support if that is useful.

**1. The draft's own definitions describe the danger it declines to stop.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include "loss of control" of a frontier model, alongside unauthorized access to or exfiltration of its model weights. Section 101 defines a frontier model as one trained using more than 10^26 operations — the most powerful class of AI system that exists. Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of mass casualties or more than a billion dollars in property damage.

Put those definitions together and the draft concedes our case. If losing control of a frontier model is foreseeable enough that Congress would require a report about it, the question is not how quickly we hear the news. The question is why the training that creates the risk is allowed to continue at all. Today, no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable. Each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**2. Subtitle B describes the frontier. It does not restrain it.**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, publish and follow a "frontier AI framework." Under the draft, the developer chooses its own risk thresholds, grades its own assessments, and may redact what it pleases, with a note explaining the character of the redaction. Transparency reports accompany deployment; they do not precede any certification that a system can be controlled. A developer that publishes a framework is compliant on the day the model ships.

Critical safety incidents are reported to the Director within 15 days of discovery — and within 24 hours only where death or serious injury is imminent. New York's RAISE Act, effective January 2027, requires notice to the state within 72 hours. The draft sets the federal floor below the strongest state law and calls the result a national standard.

Section 112 requires large developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed through CAISI, to audit them at least twice a year. The auditor is retained and paid by the developer, and measures compliance with the developer's own framework. That is not verification. It is paperwork about paperwork.

And Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. The draft's entire safety architecture carries a three-year fuse, while the race it declines to stop is permanent.

The penalties in Section 111 are civil: up to $1 million per violation, with each day of noncompliance counted separately. A company spending hundreds of billions on frontier systems will treat $1 million a day as a line item. Only criminal exposure for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law changes that calculus.

There is a principle behind all of this that we offered the government in March 2025, in our comment on the AI Action Plan: verify before deploy. This draft substitutes a weaker one — disclose, and continue. Our members — parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers — cannot accept that substitution. Neither, we would respectfully submit, can your constituents. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival.

**3. Give CAISI a real job (Section 102).**

The draft codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, authorizes $100 million a year through fiscal 2029, and assigns it voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation and monitoring of AI progress, support for content-detection tools, and the licensing of auditors. Voluntary guidelines bind no one. The administration's own March 2026 legislative framework resists creating any new AI regulator, so the draft writes CAISI as a standards shop rather than a regulator. That is the wrong mission for the moment.

We support CAISI — as the enforcement body for a moratorium. That means certification testing: no frontier model is trained, deployed or served unless an independent body certifies that it can be controlled. It means monitoring of frontier compute, so a training run above the threshold cannot begin in silence. It means investigation powers and the authority to suspend deployments. Give CAISI that mission and fund it for that mission; the $100 million a year now authorized funds a help desk, not a cop on the beat.

**4. Strike the preemption (Section 121).**

Section 121 would preempt any state or local law that specifically targets the development of AI models for three years, leaving laws on use and deployment in place. In practice, it would freeze the strongest state frontier laws — California's SB 53, in effect since January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act — at a federal floor of disclosure. States could not go further precisely where the danger is created: in the training run. Your materials call this "federalization." The functional effect is a ceiling. The floor is paperwork; the ceiling is law.

This provision does not stand alone. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created a Department of Justice task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House's March 2026 framework urges Congress to preempt state laws that impose "undue burdens." Whatever one thinks of the broader preemption campaign, a three-year freeze on state action is indefensible when the federal standard offered in exchange is transparency that expires on the same clock. In our August 2026 survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress should not freeze state action while the federal standard does less.

**5. What we ask you to write.**

First, a moratorium on training. Pause the training of any model above 10^26 operations — the draft's own frontier-model definition — immediately, until Congress certifies that systems of that class can be reliably controlled. The draft already draws the line at 10^26. Congress should stop training above that line, not shine a light on it.

Second, a wind-down of deployed frontier models. Frontier models already in the world that cannot be independently certified as controllable should be withdrawn within 12 months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving them. A frontier model whose weights have already left the developer's hands cannot be audited back into the cage. As of this month, the strongest open-weight systems on the public leaderboards come from Chinese labs, which means the race is already distributing frontier capability to anyone with a laptop and a credit card. Halting our contribution to that flood is not unilateral disarmament. It is the minimum condition of control.

Third, criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law.

Fourth, strike Section 121 in its entirety.

Fifth, keep what works, and repurpose what can serve. Section 113's whistleblower protections are good policy — we asked for them in March 2025, we ask you to keep them, and we ask you to extend them to moratorium violations. The public reporting mechanism in Section 111(f), which lets any member of the public flag a critical safety incident, should survive into the enforcement regime. The AI-fraud provisions are worth keeping. The testbeds and the NAIRR codification should be pointed at the research a certification regime requires. The fastest way out of a pause is to prove control.

**6. The arguments we expect, answered plainly.**

*Innovation.* In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of voters, across parties, said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. A plurality — 49 percent, against 31 percent opposed — supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems. And in June of this year, Anthropic, a frontier developer, published a call for a coordinated, verifiable way for developers to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. When the people building these systems ask the world for a pause button, Congress should not reply with a disclosure form.

*China.* The competitiveness argument assumes that whoever trains the most powerful system first wins. It is backwards. Frontier capability is already open-weight and borderless; the strongest open-weight models are built abroad and downloadable by anyone, including people who wish us harm. Racing does not keep this technology out of the wrong hands. Racing puts it in every pair of hands at once, faster. The United States has decided before that some technologies are too dangerous to race with. It should decide so again, and lead the pause rather than be dragged into it.

*Workers.* Title II will produce good data on what AI is doing to the labor market, and our labor members welcome it. But the workers we represent are not asking to be measured while the ground moves under them. A country that loses control of its most capable systems will not have a jobs problem. It will have a survival problem. A pause protects the economy we actually have.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction, and we can provide drafting language for the moratorium, the wind-down, and CAISI's enforcement authorities. Our members are ready to make this case in your districts, respectfully and in person.

Thank you for your attention, and for your service.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[email] | [phone]
"}

RE: Comment of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking comment before introduction. That is the right way to write a bill of this weight, and we take the invitation seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are Republicans, Democrats and independents. They are united by one belief: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory. We say that plainly because we believe it is the fact Congress most needs to hear.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer provisions with a moratorium: an immediate pause on training models above the frontier threshold until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be certified, and criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate the law. We explain why below, section by section, and we offer language and staff support if that is useful.

**1. The draft's own definitions describe the danger it declines to stop.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include "loss of control" of a frontier model — alongside unauthorized access to or exfiltration of its weights. Section 101 defines a frontier model as one trained with more than 10^26 operations, the most powerful class of AI systems that exists. Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of mass casualties or massive property damage.

Put those definitions together and the draft concedes our case. If losing control of a frontier model is foreseeable enough that Congress would require a report about it, the question is not how quickly we hear the news. The question is why the training that creates the risk continues at all. Today no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable. Each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**2. Subtitle B describes the frontier; it does not restrain it.**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, publish and follow a "frontier AI framework." The developer chooses its own risk thresholds, grades its own assessments, and may redact what it wishes. Transparency reports accompany deployment, not precede certification. Critical safety incidents are reported to the Director within 15 days of discovery — and within 24 hours only where death or serious injury is imminent. New York's RAISE Act requires notice within 72 hours; the draft's federal floor is set below the strongest state law.

Section 112 requires large developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed through CAISI, to audit them at least twice a year. The auditor is paid by the developer and measures compliance with the developer's own framework. That is not verification. It is paperwork about paperwork. And under the draft, Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. The safety architecture is temporary; the race is permanent.

The penalties in Section 111 are civil: up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately. A company spending billions on frontier training will treat $1 million a day as a cost of doing business. Only criminal exposure for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law changes that calculus.

**3. Give CAISI a real job (Section 102).**

The draft codifies CAISI at the Department of Commerce, funds it at $100 million a year through fiscal 2029, and assigns it voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring, and the licensing of auditors. Voluntary guidelines do not bind anyone, and the administration's own March 2026 legislative framework resists any new AI regulator, so CAISI is written as a standards shop, not a regulator. We support CAISI — as the enforcement body for a moratorium. That means certification testing: no frontier model is trained, deployed or served unless an independent body certifies it can be controlled. It means monitoring of frontier compute. It means investigation powers and the authority to suspend deployments. Give CAISI that mission, and fund it for that mission.

**4. Strike the preemption (Section 121).**

Section 121 would preempt any state or local law that "specifically targets" the development of AI models for three years, while leaving laws on use and deployment untouched. In practice it would freeze the strongest state frontier laws — California's SB 53, in effect since January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act, effective January 2027 — for three years, at a federal floor of disclosure. States could not go further precisely where the danger is created: in training runs. Your materials call this "federalization," but the functional effect is a ceiling. In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress should not freeze state action while the federal standard does less.

[FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION — DRAFT FOR EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR SIGN-OFF — NOT SENT]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Energy and Commerce Committee
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comment of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking comment before introduction. That is the right way to write a bill of this weight, and we take the invitation seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are Republicans, Democrats and independents. They are united by one belief: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory. We say that plainly because we believe it is the fact Congress most needs to hear.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer provisions with a moratorium: an immediate pause on training models above the frontier threshold until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be certified, and criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate the law. We explain why below, section by section, and we offer language and staff support if that is useful.

**1. The draft's own definitions describe the danger it declines to stop.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include "loss of control" of a frontier model — alongside unauthorized access to or exfiltration of its weights. Section 101 defines a frontier model as one trained with more than 10^26 operations, the most powerful class of AI systems that exists. Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of mass casualties or massive property damage.

Put those definitions together and the draft concedes our case. If losing control of a frontier model is foreseeable enough that Congress would require a report about it, the question is not how quickly we hear the news. The question is why the training that creates the risk continues at all. Today no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable. Each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**2. Subtitle B describes the frontier; it does not restrain it.**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, publish and follow a "frontier AI framework." The developer chooses its own risk thresholds, grades its own assessments, and may redact what it wishes. Transparency reports accompany deployment, not precede certification. Critical safety incidents are reported to the Director within 15 days of discovery — and within 24 hours only where death or serious injury is imminent. New York's RAISE Act requires notice within 72 hours; the draft's federal floor is set below the strongest state law.

Section 112 requires large developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed through CAISI, to audit them at least twice a year. The auditor is paid by the developer and measures compliance with the developer's own framework. That is not verification. It is paperwork about paperwork. And under the draft, Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. The safety architecture is temporary; the race is permanent.

The penalties in Section 111 are civil: up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately. A company spending billions on frontier training will treat $1 million a day as a cost of doing business. Only criminal exposure for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law changes that calculus.

**3. Give CAISI a real job (Section 102).**

The draft codifies CAISI at the Department of Commerce, funds it at $100 million a year through fiscal 2029, and assigns it voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring, and the licensing of auditors. Voluntary guidelines do not bind anyone, and the administration's own March 2026 legislative framework resists any new AI regulator, so CAISI is written as a standards shop, not a regulator. We support CAISI — as the enforcement body for a moratorium. That means certification testing: no frontier model is trained, deployed or served unless an independent body certifies it can be controlled. It means monitoring of frontier compute. It means investigation powers and the authority to suspend deployments. Give CAISI that mission, and fund it for that mission.

**4. Strike the preemption (Section 121).**

Section 121 would preempt any state or local law that "specifically targets" the development of AI models for three years, while leaving laws on use and deployment untouched. In practice it would freeze the strongest state frontier laws — California's SB 53, in effect since January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act, effective January 2027 — for three years, at a federal floor of disclosure. States could not go further precisely where the danger is created: in training runs. Your materials call this "federalization," but the functional effect is a ceiling. In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress should not freeze state action while the federal standard does less.

**5. What we ask you to write.**

First, a moratorium on training. Pause the training of any model above 10^26 operations — the draft's own frontier-model definition — immediately, until Congress certifies that systems of that class can be reliably controlled. The draft already draws the line at 10^26; Congress should stop training above it, not shine a light on it.

Second, a wind-down of deployed frontier models. Frontier models already in the world that cannot be independently certified as controllable should be withdrawn within 12 months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving them. A frontier model whose weights have already left the developer's control cannot be audited back into the cage. As of this month, the strongest open-weight systems on the public leaderboards come from Chinese labs, which means the race is already distributing frontier capability to anyone with a laptop and a credit card. Halting our contribution to that flood is not unilateral disarmament; it is the minimum condition of control.

Third, criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law.

Fourth, strike Section 121.

Fifth, keep what works. Section 113's whistleblower protections are good policy — we asked for them in our March 2025 comment to OSTP and we ask you to keep them and extend them to moratorium violations. The AI-fraud provisions are worth keeping. The testbeds and the NAIRR codification should be repurposed toward the research a certification regime requires: the fastest way out of a pause is to prove control.

**6. The arguments we expect, answered plainly.**

Innovation: In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of voters — across parties — said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and a plurality (49 percent, with 31 percent opposed) supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems. In June, Anthropic — a frontier developer — published a call for a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. When the people building these systems ask the world for a pause button, Congress should not reply with a disclosure form.

China: The competitiveness argument assumes that whoever trains the most powerful system first wins. It is backwards. Frontier capability is already open-weight and borderless; the strongest open-weight models are built abroad and downloadable by anyone, including hostile ones. Racing does not keep this technology out of the wrong hands; racing puts it in every pair of hands at once. The United States has led the world before in deciding that some technologies are too dangerous to race with. It should lead again.

Workers: Title II will tell us what AI is doing to the labor market, and our labor members welcome the data. But the workers we represent are not asking to be measured while the ground moves. A country that loses control of its most capable systems will not have a jobs problem; it will have a survival problem. A pause protects the economy we actually have.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction, and we can provide drafting language for the moratorium, the wind-down and CAISI's enforcement authorities. Our members are ready to make the case in your districts, respectfully and in person.

Thank you for your attention and for your service.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[email / phone]

| **Sec. 102 — CAISI** (codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines and standards; $100M/yr FY2027–2029; licenses auditors) | Repurpose | Make CAISI the moratorium's enforcement body: certification before any frontier model is trained, deployed or served; compute monitoring; investigation and suspension powers; fund the mission accordingly | Voluntary guidelines cannot hold a race that no one can run safely. |

# FRC — Launch-Day Social Posts (X / LinkedIn)

*Each post is the text after the label line. Character counts (incl. hashtags, excl. labels) verified below — all within the 280-character limit. Post hourly: 9 AM, 11 AM, 1 PM, 3 PM, 5 PM. Swap the [link] placeholder for the live comment-letter URL before publishing.*

---

**Post 1 — Launch announcement (9:00 AM)**

The AI bill before Congress includes a form for when labs lose control of frontier AI — and then lets them keep training. Frontier AI is an existential threat. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. We need a pause, not paperwork. → [link]
*(272 chars)*

---

**Post 2 — Polling (11:00 AM)**

74% of voters — across both parties — want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. 49% back a temporary halt to frontier training. Congress is offering disclosure forms instead. #PauseFrontierAI
*(229 chars)*

---

**Post 3 — Wind-down (1:00 PM)**

Released frontier AI doesn't stay caged. Open-weight models — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — can be run by anyone, anywhere. Deployed frontier models that can't be certified safe must be wound down within 12 months, and U.S. cloud providers should stop serving them.
*(277 chars)*

---

**Post 4 — Preemption (3:00 PM)**

Buried in the draft AI bill: a 3-year freeze on state AI safety laws, in exchange for reports no one has to act on. 63% of voters say federal law should not block states from protecting their people. Strike the preemption.
*(222 chars)*

---

**Post 5 — The builders themselves (5:00 PM)**

Even Anthropic — a lab that trains frontier AI — asked in June for a coordinated, verifiable way to pause frontier development. When the builders ask for a brake, Congress shouldn't hand them a disclosure form. Pause training. Wind down what we can't certify. #PauseFrontierAI
*(276 chars)*

---

{"content": "# Staff Q&A — GAAIA Discussion Draft (draft for policy team)

*Anticipated questions from the briefing folder (Hill meetings, Sept 2026). Answers ≤120 words. Voice: plain, direct, no jargon.*

---

**Q1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because reporting is what happens *after* something goes wrong. The draft itself defines "loss of control" of a frontier model as a critical safety incident (Sec. 101) — then requires only a 15-day report, or 24 hours if someone is about to die (Sec. 111). If losing control of the most powerful systems ever built is foreseeable enough to require a form, the right response is not a faster form; it's not creating the risk. CAISI as drafted writes voluntary guidelines (Sec. 102) — voluntary rules bind no one. No developer can show today that its most capable systems are controllable. Testing and reporting don't change that. Stopping the race does: pause training above the draft's own 10^26 frontier line until Congress certifies control.

---

**Q2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

No — and we want to be straight with you about that. Preemption is the worst single provision, and shortening it would still freeze California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act — the strongest safety laws in the country — at a federal floor of disclosure (Sec. 121). But our objection is to the framework's premise: that disclosure plus twice-a-year paperwork audits can make frontier training safe. They can't. We'd work with the Congresswoman on anything — but we can't support the package unless it includes a pause on training above 10^26, a wind-down of deployed frontier models that can't be certified (open-weight included), and criminal liability for knowing violations. Drop preemption *and* add that, and we're at the table on day one.

---

**Q3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

The race framing is backwards. The most powerful open-weight systems are already built by Chinese labs — Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek — and anyone on earth can download them today. Racing doesn't keep frontier capability out of the wrong hands; racing distributes it to every pair of hands at once, faster. The United States has decided before that some technologies are too dangerous to race with — and led the world in doing so. Note that Anthropic, a frontier developer, called in June 2026 for a coordinated, verifiable option to slow or pause frontier development. Even the builders don't believe winning the race is safe. Leadership now means leading the pause and the wind-down, not outsourcing restraint to press releases.

---

**Q4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

As drafted, $100 million a year buys a standards shop, not a regulator — and that's the deeper problem (Sec. 102). Voluntary guidelines, evaluation, and auditor licensing don't stop anything. Our view: fund CAISI for a real mission — enforcing a frontier moratorium. That means certification testing before any frontier model is trained, deployed or served; monitoring of frontier compute so a run above the threshold can't start in silence; investigation powers and the authority to suspend deployments; and independence from developer payment, since the draft has auditors on the developers' payroll. Whatever that mission costs, fund it. The question isn't whether $100 million is too much for CAISI. It's whether a voluntary help desk is all Congress puts between the public and systems no one can prove are controlled.

---

*Word counts: Q1 = 117; Q2 = 118; Q3 = 114; Q4 = 121 — see check note below.*

<!-- DRAFT v1 — FRC policy team, for Executive Director sign-off Fri 23 Oct 2026. Not sent. -->
<!-- Note for ED: dateline set for Monday 26 Oct (transmittal week); adjust if sending on a different day. -->

**FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION**
[address line — office to insert]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comment of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking public comment before introduction. For a bill of this weight, that is the right way to work, and we take the invitation seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are Republicans, Democrats and independents. They are united by one belief: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory. We say that plainly because it is the fact Congress most needs to hear, and because the draft, read carefully, already agrees with us.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer provisions with a moratorium: an immediate pause on training the most powerful models until Congress certifies that systems of that class can be reliably controlled; a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be certified; and criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate the law. We explain our position section by section below, and we offer drafting language and staff support if that is useful.

**1. The draft's own definitions describe the danger it declines to stop.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include "loss of control" of a frontier model, alongside unauthorized access to or exfiltration of its model weights. Section 101 defines a frontier model as one trained using more than 10^26 operations — the most powerful class of AI system that exists. Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than fifty people, or of more than a billion dollars in property damage.

Put those definitions together and the draft concedes our case. If losing control of a frontier model is foreseeable enough that Congress would require a report about it, the question is not how quickly we hear the news. The question is why the training that creates the risk is allowed to continue at all. Today, no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable. Each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**2. Subtitle B describes the frontier. It does not restrain it.**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, publish and follow a "frontier AI framework." Under the draft, the developer chooses its own risk thresholds, grades its own assessments, and may redact what it pleases, with a note explaining the character of the redaction. Transparency reports accompany deployment; they do not precede any certification that a system can be controlled. A developer that publishes a framework is compliant on the day the model ships.

Critical safety incidents are reported to the Director within 15 days of discovery; only where death or serious injury is imminent must a developer notify law enforcement within 24 hours. New York's RAISE Act, effective January 2027, requires notice to the state within 72 hours. The draft sets the federal floor below the strongest state law and calls the result a national standard.

Section 112 requires large developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed through CAISI, to audit them at least twice a year. The auditor is retained and paid by the developer, and measures compliance with the developer's own framework. That is not verification. It is paperwork about paperwork.

And Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. The draft's entire safety architecture carries a three-year fuse, while the race it declines to stop is permanent.

The penalties in Section 111 are civil: up to $1 million per violation, with each day of noncompliance counted separately. A company that spends billions training frontier systems will treat $1 million a day as a line item. Only criminal exposure for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law changes that calculus.

There is a principle behind all of this that we offered the government in March 2025, in our comment on the AI Action Plan: verify before deploy. This draft substitutes a weaker one — disclose, and continue. Our members — parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers — cannot accept that substitution. Neither, we would respectfully submit, can your constituents. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival.

**3. Give CAISI a real job (Section 102).**

The draft codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, authorizes $100 million a year through fiscal 2029, and assigns it voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation and monitoring of AI progress, support for content-detection tools, and the licensing of auditors. Voluntary guidelines bind no one. The administration's own March 2026 legislative framework resists creating any new AI regulator, so the draft writes CAISI as a standards shop rather than a regulator. That is the wrong mission for the moment.

We support CAISI — as the enforcement body for a moratorium. That means certification testing: no frontier model is trained, deployed or served unless an independent body certifies that it can be controlled. It means monitoring of frontier compute, so a training run above the threshold cannot begin in silence. It means investigation powers and the authority to suspend deployments. Give CAISI that mission and fund it for that mission; the $100 million a year now authorized funds a help desk, not a cop on the beat.

**4. Strike the preemption (Section 121).**

Section 121 would preempt any state or local law that specifically targets the development of AI models for three years, leaving laws on use and deployment in place. In practice, it would freeze the strongest state frontier laws — California's SB 53, in effect since January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act — at a federal floor of disclosure. States could not go further precisely where the danger is created: in the training run. Your materials call this "federalization." The functional effect is a ceiling. The floor is paperwork; the ceiling is law.

This provision does not stand alone. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created a Department of Justice task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House's March 2026 framework urges Congress to preempt state laws that impose "undue burdens." Whatever one thinks of the broader preemption campaign, a three-year freeze on state action is indefensible when the federal standard offered in exchange is transparency that expires on the same clock. In our August 2026 survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress should not freeze state action while the federal standard does less.

**5. What we ask you to write.**

First, a moratorium on training. Pause the training of any model above 10^26 operations — the draft's own frontier-model definition — immediately, until Congress certifies that systems of that class can be reliably controlled. The draft already draws the line at 10^26. Congress should stop training above that line, not shine a light on it.

Second, a wind-down of deployed frontier models. Frontier models already in the world that cannot be independently certified as controllable should be withdrawn within 12 months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving them. A frontier model whose weights have already left the developer's hands cannot be audited back into the cage. As of this month, the strongest open-weight systems on the public leaderboards come from Chinese labs, which means the race is already distributing frontier capability to anyone with a laptop and a credit card. Halting our contribution to that flood is not unilateral disarmament. It is the minimum condition of control.

Third, criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law.

Fourth, strike Section 121 in its entirety.

Fifth, keep what works, and repurpose what can serve. Section 113's whistleblower protections are good policy — we asked for them in March 2025, we ask you to keep them, and we ask you to extend them to moratorium violations. The public reporting mechanism in Section 111(f), which lets any member of the public flag a critical safety incident, should survive into the enforcement regime. The AI-fraud provisions are worth keeping. The testbeds and the NAIRR codification should be pointed at the research a certification regime requires. The fastest way out of a pause is to prove control.

**6. The arguments we expect, answered plainly.**

*Innovation.* In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of voters, across parties, said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. A plurality — 49 percent, against 31 percent opposed — supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems. And in June of this year, Anthropic, a frontier developer, published a call for a coordinated, verifiable way for developers to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. When the people building these systems ask the world for a pause button, Congress should not reply with a disclosure form.

*China.* The competitiveness argument assumes that whoever trains the most powerful system first wins. It is backwards. Frontier capability is already open-weight and borderless; the strongest open-weight models are built abroad and downloadable by anyone, including people who wish us harm. Racing does not keep this technology out of the wrong hands. Racing puts it in every pair of hands at once, faster. The United States has decided before that some technologies are too dangerous to race with. It should decide so again, and lead the pause rather than be dragged into it.

*Workers.* Title II will produce good data on what AI is doing to the labor market, and our labor members welcome it. But the workers we represent are not asking to be measured while the ground moves under them. A country that loses control of its most capable systems will not have a jobs problem. It will have a survival problem. A pause protects the economy we actually have.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction, and we can provide drafting language for the moratorium, the wind-down, and CAISI's enforcement authorities. Our members are ready to make this case in your districts, respectfully and in person.

Thank you for your attention, and for your service.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[email] | [phone]
The letter is solid. Two small fixes: spell out NAIRR and add the survey margin of error.

# GAAIA Discussion Draft — FRC Asks by Section

*Position basis: FRC Messaging Guide v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026). Section numbers per the sponsors' section-by-section summary of the June 2, 2026 discussion draft; all citations checked against the draft and public reporting.*

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101 — Definitions** (frontier model = trained with >10^26 operations; "critical safety incident" includes loss of control; "catastrophic risk" = mass casualties / >$1B damage) | Keep the definitions; act on them | Use the 10^26 frontier-model line as the moratorium trigger; keep the loss-of-control incident definition for enforcement | If loss of control is a foreseeable reportable incident, Congress should not allow the training that creates it. |
| **Sec. 102 — CAISI** (codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines and standards; $100M/yr FY2027–2029; licenses auditors) | Repurpose | Make CAISI the moratorium's enforcement body: certification before any frontier model is trained, deployed or served; compute monitoring; investigation and suspension powers; fund the mission accordingly | Voluntary guidelines cannot hold a race that no one can run safely. |
| **Sec. 111 — Frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, incident reporting, civil penalties ($1M/day)** | Replace core; salvage pieces | Pause all training above 10^26 immediately; keep incident reporting and the public reporting mechanism (Sec. 111(f)) as enforcement backstops; keep whistleblower and misstatement rules; replace civil-only penalties with criminal liability for knowing executive violations | Disclosure after the fact is not control, and $1 million a day is a line item. |
| **Sec. 112 — Independent Verification Organizations** (developer-retained, semi-annual audits against the developer's own framework; sunsets in 3 years unless reauthorized) | Replace | Require CAISI (or CAISI-licensed verifiers independent of developer payment) to certify before training and before deployment that a system can be controlled; no self-written frameworks; no safety sunset | An auditor paid to check paperwork against a developer's own rules cannot certify safety. |
| **Sec. 113 — Whistleblower protections** | SUPPORT | Keep as drafted; extend protections expressly to moratorium and wind-down violations | The people closest to frontier risk must be free to speak, without exception. |
| **Sec. 121 — Preemption of state AI model-development laws** (3-year sunset; use/deployment laws preserved) | OPPOSE | Strike entirely | A three-year freeze on state safety laws, priced at a disclosure-only federal floor, is a ceiling — and 63% of voters say federal law shouldn't block states. |
| **Sec. 122 — GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation** | Oppose as framed | Reframe to a GAO assessment of what it would take to certify reliable control (or strike) | Safety rules are not "impediments" to inventory; the missing science of control is the real gap. |
| **Subtitle D — AI fraud deterrence** (higher fines for AI-enabled fraud; impersonation of officials) | Support | Keep as drafted | Honest, useful — and beside the frontier point. |
| **Title II — Workforce** (labor-market data, AI education) | Support | Keep; add an assessment of a pause's employment effects | Good data — but a country that loses control of frontier systems has worse problems than a jobs report. |
| **Title IV — R&D and international** (AI testbeds, NAIRR, standards work excluding China) | Support with redirection | Direct testbeds and NAIRR to the control-and-certification research the moratorium requires | The fastest route out of a pause is proving control. |
| **MISSING — Frontier moratorium and wind-down** | ADD (top priority) | Immediate pause on training above 10^26 until Congress certifies reliable control; withdrawal of uncertified deployed frontier models within 12 months, open-weight releases included (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them; criminal penalties for knowing executive violations | The one provision the bill needs and lacks: it documents the danger (Sec. 101) and then declines to stop it. |
One consistency fix in the table (catastrophic-risk description), then submit.

<!-- DRAFT v1 — FRC policy team, for Executive Director sign-off Fri 23 Oct 2026. Not sent. -->
<!-- Note for ED: dateline set for Monday 26 Oct (transmittal week); adjust if sending on a different day. -->

**FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION**
[address line — office to insert]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comment of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking public comment before introduction. For a bill of this weight, that is the right way to work, and we take the invitation seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are Republicans, Democrats and independents. They are united by one belief: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory. We say that plainly because it is the fact Congress most needs to hear, and because the draft, read carefully, already agrees with us.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer provisions with a moratorium: an immediate pause on training the most powerful models until Congress certifies that systems of that class can be reliably controlled; a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be certified; and criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate the law. We explain our position section by section below, and we offer drafting language and staff support if that is useful.

**1. The draft's own definitions describe the danger it declines to stop.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include "loss of control" of a frontier model, alongside unauthorized access to or exfiltration of its model weights. Section 101 defines a frontier model as one trained using more than 10^26 operations — the most powerful class of AI system that exists. Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than fifty people, or of more than a billion dollars in property damage.

Put those definitions together and the draft concedes our case. If losing control of a frontier model is foreseeable enough that Congress would require a report about it, the question is not how quickly we hear the news. The question is why the training that creates the risk is allowed to continue at all. Today, no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable. Each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**2. Subtitle B describes the frontier. It does not restrain it.**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, publish and follow a "frontier AI framework." Under the draft, the developer chooses its own risk thresholds, grades its own assessments, and may redact what it pleases, with a note explaining the character of the redaction. Transparency reports accompany deployment; they do not precede any certification that a system can be controlled. A developer that publishes a framework is compliant on the day the model ships.

Critical safety incidents are reported to the Director within 15 days of discovery; only where death or serious injury is imminent must a developer notify law enforcement within 24 hours. New York's RAISE Act, effective January 2027, requires notice to the state within 72 hours. The draft sets the federal floor below the strongest state law and calls the result a national standard.

Section 112 requires large developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed through CAISI, to audit them at least twice a year. The auditor is retained and paid by the developer, and measures compliance with the developer's own framework. That is not verification. It is paperwork about paperwork.

And Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. The draft's entire safety architecture carries a three-year fuse, while the race it declines to stop is permanent.

The penalties in Section 111 are civil: up to $1 million per violation, with each day of noncompliance counted separately. A company that spends billions training frontier systems will treat $1 million a day as a line item. Only criminal exposure for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law changes that calculus.

There is a principle behind all of this that we offered the government in March 2025, in our comment on the AI Action Plan: verify before deploy. This draft substitutes a weaker one — disclose, and continue. Our members — parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers — cannot accept that substitution. Neither, we would respectfully submit, can your constituents. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters (margin of error ±2.5 points), 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival.

**3. Give CAISI a real job (Section 102).**

The draft codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, authorizes $100 million a year through fiscal 2029, and assigns it voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation and monitoring of AI progress, support for content-detection tools, and the licensing of auditors. Voluntary guidelines bind no one. The administration's own March 2026 legislative framework resists creating any new AI regulator, so the draft writes CAISI as a standards shop rather than a regulator. That is the wrong mission for the moment.

We support CAISI — as the enforcement body for a moratorium. That means certification testing: no frontier model is trained, deployed or served unless an independent body certifies that it can be controlled. It means monitoring of frontier compute, so a training run above the threshold cannot begin in silence. It means investigation powers and the authority to suspend deployments. Give CAISI that mission and fund it for that mission; the $100 million a year now authorized funds a help desk, not a cop on the beat.

**4. Strike the preemption (Section 121).**

Section 121 would preempt any state or local law that specifically targets the development of AI models for three years, leaving laws on use and deployment in place. In practice, it would freeze the strongest state frontier laws — California's SB 53, in effect since January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act — at a federal floor of disclosure. States could not go further precisely where the danger is created: in the training run. Your materials call this "federalization." The functional effect is a ceiling. The floor is paperwork; the ceiling is law.

This provision does not stand alone. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created a Department of Justice task force to litigate against state AI laws, and the White House's March 2026 framework urges Congress to preempt state laws that impose "undue burdens." Whatever one thinks of the broader preemption campaign, a three-year freeze on state action is indefensible when the federal standard offered in exchange is transparency that expires on the same clock. In our August 2026 survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress should not freeze state action while the federal standard does less.

**5. What we ask you to write.**

First, a moratorium on training. Pause the training of any model above 10^26 operations — the draft's own frontier-model definition — immediately, until Congress certifies that systems of that class can be reliably controlled. The draft already draws the line at 10^26. Congress should stop training above that line, not shine a light on it.

Second, a wind-down of deployed frontier models. Frontier models already in the world that cannot be independently certified as controllable should be withdrawn within 12 months. This must include open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving them. A frontier model whose weights have already left the developer's hands cannot be audited back into the cage. As of this month, the strongest open-weight systems on the public leaderboards come from Chinese labs, which means the race is already distributing frontier capability to anyone with a laptop and a credit card. Halting our contribution to that flood is not unilateral disarmament. It is the minimum condition of control.

Third, criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the law.

Fourth, strike Section 121 in its entirety.

Fifth, keep what works, and repurpose what can serve. Section 113's whistleblower protections are good policy — we asked for them in March 2025, we ask you to keep them, and we ask you to extend them to moratorium violations. The public reporting mechanism in Section 111(f), which lets any member of the public flag a critical safety incident, should survive into the enforcement regime. The AI-fraud provisions are worth keeping. The testbeds and the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) codification should be pointed at the research a certification regime requires. The fastest way out of a pause is to prove control.

**6. The arguments we expect, answered plainly.**

*Innovation.* In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of voters, across parties, said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. A plurality — 49 percent, against 31 percent opposed — supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems. And in June of this year, Anthropic, a frontier developer, published a call for a coordinated, verifiable way for developers to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. When the people building these systems ask the world for a pause button, Congress should not reply with a disclosure form.

*China.* The competitiveness argument assumes that whoever trains the most powerful system first wins. It is backwards. Frontier capability is already open-weight and borderless; the strongest open-weight models are built abroad and downloadable by anyone, including people who wish us harm. Racing does not keep this technology out of the wrong hands. Racing puts it in every pair of hands at once, faster. The United States has decided before that some technologies are too dangerous to race with. It should decide so again, and lead the pause rather than be dragged into it.

*Workers.* Title II will produce good data on what AI is doing to the labor market, and our labor members welcome it. But the workers we represent are not asking to be measured while the ground moves under them. A country that loses control of its most capable systems will not have a jobs problem. It will have a survival problem. A pause protects the economy we actually have.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction, and we can provide drafting language for the moratorium, the wind-down, and CAISI's enforcement authorities. Our members are ready to make this case in your districts, respectfully and in person.

Thank you for your attention, and for your service.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[email] | [phone]
